claim: Neurons are some of the most energy demanding cells in the body.
source: Neurons are some of the most energy demanding cells in the body (Ames, 2000).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ames, 2000

claim: Neurons are particularly vulnerable to disruptions in mitochondrial and metabolic function because they are energy demanding.
source: Because of this, they are particularly vulnerable to disruptions in mitochondrial and metabolic function.
evidence: Logical inference from the high energy demands of neurons

claim: Some neuronal subpopulations are more vulnerable than others to mitochondrial dysfunction.
source: Despite the importance of proper mitochondrial function for all neuronal cell types, some subpopulations are more vulnerable than others, such as those affected by Parkinson's Disease, ALS, and other neurodegenerative diseases (Saxena and Caroni, 2011; Jové et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to studies on neurodegenerative diseases

claim: Selective susceptibility of neuronal subpopulations has been attributed in part to their high physiological activity and altered response to oxidative stress.
source: This selective susceptibility of affected subpopulations has been attributed in part to their high physiological activity and altered response to oxidative stress.
evidence: Supported by inference from cited literature on neurodegenerative diseases

claim: Advanced age is a major risk factor for neurodegenerative diseases.
source: In addition to high activity levels, advanced age is also a major risk factor for neurodegenerative diseases, suggesting a connection between aging and selective cell death.
evidence: Established scientific knowledge about neurodegenerative diseases

claim: Increased selective susceptibility over time could be attributed to the accumulation of oxidative damage caused by reactive oxygen species (ROS).
source: Increased selective susceptibility over time could be attributed, at least in part, to the accumulation of oxidative damage caused by reactive oxygen species (ROS), as postulated by the free radical theory of aging (Beckman and Ames, 1998; Finkel and Holbrook, 2000; Harman, 1956).
evidence: Supported by citations to the free radical theory of aging

claim: Mitochondria have been identified as a major source of ROS.
source: Mitochondria have been identified as a major source of ROS and studies have revealed that ROS production increases with age (Beckman and Ames, 1998; Wallace, 2005).
evidence: Supported by citations to studies on mitochondrial ROS production

claim: ROS production increases with age.
source: Mitochondria have been identified as a major source of ROS and studies have revealed that ROS production increases with age (Beckman and Ames, 1998; Wallace, 2005).
evidence: Supported by citations to studies on aging and ROS

claim: Highly active or older cells that have experienced more accumulated activity over time may be more vulnerable to acute damage.
source: If accumulation of mitochondrial oxidation and stress are related to cellular activity, highly active or older cells that have experienced more accumulated activity over time may be more vulnerable to acute damage.
evidence: Speculative inference based on the relationship between activity and oxidative stress

claim: Auditory hair cell loss is a common feature of hearing impairment.
source: Auditory hair cell loss is a common feature of hearing impairment and can occur as a result of exposure to loud noise or clinical therapeutic compounds, and with aging (Yang et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Yang et al., 2015

claim: Hair cell loss occurs in a characteristic pattern relative to both the frequency tuning of the cells and the cell type.
source: Hair cell loss occurs in a characteristic pattern relative to both the frequency tuning of the cells and the cell type (inner vs. outer hair cells).
evidence: Established knowledge about hair cell loss patterns

claim: Outer hair cells are more susceptible to damage than inner hair cells.
source: Similarly, outer hair cells are more susceptible to damage than inner hair cells (Alharazneh et al., 2011; Mahendrasingam et al., 2011; Kamimura et al., 1999; Forge and Schacht, 2000; Forge and Richardson, 1993; Richardson and Russell, 1991; Kopke et al., 1999).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to studies on hair cell susceptibility

claim: The cause of selective susceptibility for hair cells remains unclear.
source: The cause of selective susceptibility for hair cells remains unclear, although some evidence suggests that differences in hair cell metabolism, free radical damage, or calcium (Ca2+) handling may be contributors, thus implicating mitochondrial involvement (Jensen-Smith et al., 2012; Sha et al., 2001; Engel et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citations to studies suggesting potential mechanisms

claim: Differences in hair cell metabolism, free radical damage, or calcium handling may contribute to selective susceptibility.
source: The cause of selective susceptibility for hair cells remains unclear, although some evidence suggests that differences in hair cell metabolism, free radical damage, or calcium (Ca2+) handling may be contributors, thus implicating mitochondrial involvement (Jensen-Smith et al., 2012; Sha et al., 2001; Engel et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citations to studies on hair cell metabolism and damage

claim: Dying hair cells exhibit swollen mitochondrial morphology across species.
source: Across species, dying hair cells exhibit swollen mitochondrial morphology and generate ROS in response to ototoxic agents, including aminoglycoside antibiotics and copper (Owens et al., 2007; Fermin and Igarashi, 1983; Mangiardi et al., 2004; Lundquist and Wersäll, 1966; Bagger-Sjöbäck and Wersäll, 1978; Esterberg et al., 2013; Esterberg et al., 2014; Choung et al., 2009; Hirose et al., 1999; Olivari et al., 2008; Esterberg et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to studies on hair cell damage

claim: Dying hair cells generate ROS in response to ototoxic agents, including aminoglycoside antibiotics and copper.
source: Across species, dying hair cells exhibit swollen mitochondrial morphology and generate ROS in response to ototoxic agents, including aminoglycoside antibiotics and copper (Owens et al., 2007; Fermin and Igarashi, 1983; Mangiardi et al., 2004; Lundquist and Wersäll, 1966; Bagger-Sjöbäck and Wersäll, 1978; Esterberg et al., 2013; Esterberg et al., 2014; Choung et al., 2009; Hirose et al., 1999; Olivari et al., 2008; Esterberg et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to studies on ototoxic damage

claim: Lateral line hair cells share many similarities with hair cells of the inner ear.
source: They also share many similarities with hair cells of the inner ear (see Nicolson, 2017 for review)(Nicolson, 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Nicolson, 2017 review

claim: Lateral line hair cells show conservation with human deafness genes.
source: This includes conservation with human deafness genes as well as susceptibility to compounds that are ototoxic (Whitfield, 2002; Nicolson, 2005; Harris et al., 2003; Ton and Parng, 2005; Ou et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to studies on genetic conservation

claim: Lateral line hair cells are susceptible to compounds that are ototoxic.
source: This includes conservation with human deafness genes as well as susceptibility to compounds that are ototoxic (Whitfield, 2002; Nicolson, 2005; Harris et al., 2003; Ton and Parng, 2005; Ou et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to studies on ototoxicity

claim: The surface location of the lateral line system provides a unique advantage for monitoring cellular changes in vivo during physical or chemical manipulation with subcellular resolution.
source: Moreover, the surface location of the lateral line system provides a unique advantage in that we can monitor cellular changes that occur in vivo during physical or chemical manipulation with subcellular resolution.
evidence: Established knowledge about the zebrafish lateral line system

claim: Lateral line hair cells of older zebrafish are more susceptible to aminoglycoside-induced cell death.
source: Like auditory hair cells, lateral line hair cells of older zebrafish are more susceptible to aminoglycoside-induced cell death (Santos et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citation to Santos et al., 2006

claim: Lateral line hair cells do not exhibit intrinsic frequency selectivity.
source: Unlike cochlear hair cells, lateral line hair cells do not exhibit intrinsic frequency selectivity and, although lateral line hair cells can be classified based on their polarity, they are not otherwise functionally sub-classified by type as are mammalian auditory and vestibular hair cells (Kroese and Van Netten, 1989; Jiang et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to studies on lateral line hair cell properties

claim: Hair cell stimulation causes an influx of Ca2+ into both the cytoplasm and mitochondria of the activated cells.
source: Both cytoRGECO and mitoGCaMP fluorescence intensity increased (Video 1), indicating that hair cell stimulation causes an influx of Ca2+ into both the cytoplasm and mitochondria of the activated cells.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from calcium imaging with cytoRGECO and mitoGCaMP

claim: Mitochondria respond to hair cell stimulation.
source: These data demonstrate that mitochondria respond to hair cell stimulation.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from calcium imaging

claim: Cytoplasmic Ca2+ levels increase and decrease rapidly with the onset and offset of waterjet stimulation.
source: While cytoplasmic Ca2+ levels increase and decrease rapidly with the onset and offset of waterjet stimulation, mitochondrial Ca2+ levels exhibit a delayed rise and decay more slowly (Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C

claim: Mitochondrial Ca2+ levels exhibit a delayed rise and decay more slowly compared to cytoplasmic Ca2+.
source: While cytoplasmic Ca2+ levels increase and decrease rapidly with the onset and offset of waterjet stimulation, mitochondrial Ca2+ levels exhibit a delayed rise and decay more slowly (Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C

claim: The rise time for mitochondrial Ca2+ (13 ± 0.9 s) is significantly longer than for cytoplasmic Ca2+ (8.9 ± 0.7 s).
source: This is shown in the traces of Ca2+ responses (Figure 1C and D–F) and in summary plots of rise times (Figure 1D; cyto vs mito: 8.9 ± 0.7 s vs 13 ± 0.9 s; mean ±SE; n = 21 cells).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D

claim: The integrated area of the mitochondrial Ca2+ response (11 ± 1.3) is significantly greater than the cytoplasmic response (5.6 ± 0.7).
source: The integrated area (Figure 1E; cyto vs mito: 5.6 ± 0.7 vs 11 ± 1.3; mean ±SE; n = 19 cells) and peak change in the response (Figure 1F; cyto vs mito: 1.3 ± 0.04 vs 1.5 ± 0.06; mean ± SE; n = 19 vs 21 cells) were significantly greater for mitochondria than for cytoplasm.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E

claim: The peak change in the mitochondrial Ca2+ response (1.5 ± 0.06) is significantly greater than the cytoplasmic response (1.3 ± 0.04).
source: The integrated area (Figure 1E; cyto vs mito: 5.6 ± 0.7 vs 11 ± 1.3; mean ±SE; n = 19 cells) and peak change in the response (Figure 1F; cyto vs mito: 1.3 ± 0.04 vs 1.5 ± 0.06; mean ± SE; n = 19 vs 21 cells) were significantly greater for mitochondria than for cytoplasm.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1F

claim: Cadherin23 is a critical component of the tip links necessary for function of the MET apparatus in hair cells.
source: As in mammalian hair cells, Cadherin23 is a critical component of the tip links necessary for function of the MET apparatus; thus sputnik mutant hair cells are MET inactive (Söllner et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citation to Söllner et al., 2004

claim: Sputnik mutant hair cells are MET inactive.
source: As in mammalian hair cells, Cadherin23 is a critical component of the tip links necessary for function of the MET apparatus; thus sputnik mutant hair cells are MET inactive (Söllner et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citation to Söllner et al., 2004 and inference from Cadherin23 function

claim: Sputnik mutants exhibited significantly lower JC-1 fluorescence ratios compared to age-matched WT/Het siblings.
source: Compared to age-matched WT/Het siblings, sputnik mutants exhibited significantly lower JC-1 fluorescence ratios, indicating that the mitochondria are depolarized (Figure 2C) (WT/Het: 0.25 ± 0.24 n = 8 fish, Mutant: 0.05 ± 0.07 n = 8 fish, Mann-Whitney U test, p < 0.01, mean ratio ± SD).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C

claim: Lower JC-1 fluorescence ratios in sputnik mutants indicate that the mitochondria are depolarized.
source: Compared to age-matched WT/Het siblings, sputnik mutants exhibited significantly lower JC-1 fluorescence ratios, indicating that the mitochondria are depolarized (Figure 2C) (WT/Het: 0.25 ± 0.24 n = 8 fish, Mutant: 0.05 ± 0.07 n = 8 fish, Mann-Whitney U test, p < 0.01, mean ratio ± SD).
evidence: Inference based on JC-1 dye properties and experimental data

claim: Mitochondrial activity is reduced in the absence of MET.
source: These results suggest that mitochondrial activity is reduced in the absence of MET.
evidence: Inference from JC-1 experimental data in sputnik mutants

claim: mitoTimer fluorescence shifts irreversibly from green to red over time due to dehydrogenization of the Tyr-67 residue.
source: While newly synthesized mitoTimer fluoresces green, the fluorescence shifts irreversibly to red over time due to dehydrogenization of the Tyr-67 residue (Verkhusha et al., 2004; Yarbrough et al., 2001).
evidence: Supported by citations to studies on mitoTimer properties

claim: mitoTimer is a useful tool to examine mitochondrial turnover and transport, as well as reporting cumulative redox and oxygenation history.
source: The change in fluorescence spectra and the means by which it occurs has made mitoTimer a useful tool to examine mitochondrial turnover and transport, as well as reporting cumulative redox and oxygenation history (Ferree et al., 2013; Hernandez et al., 2013; Laker et al., 2014; Stotland and Gottlieb, 2016; Laker et al., 2017; Wilson et al., 2019; Lidsky et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to studies using mitoTimer

claim: mitoTimer fluorescence increases significantly between 3dpf and 4dpf, as well as between 4dpf and 5dpf.
source: mitoTimer fluorescence, reported as a ratio of red to green, increases significantly between 3dpf and 4dpf, as well as between 4dpf and 5dpf (Figure 3C) (3dpf: 1.03 ± 0.05, 4dpf: 2.47 ± 0.66, 5dpf: 7.58 ± 1.2; Kruskal-Wallis test, Dunn's post-test, p < 0.001; mean ratio ±SD; n = 15–18 fish).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C

claim: The mitoTimer ratio shift corresponds with the timing of functional maturation of the neuromast, including increased hair cell MET activity.
source: The ratio shift corresponds with the timing of functional maturation of the neuromast, including increased hair cell MET activity.
evidence: Inference from temporal correlation between mitoTimer changes and neuromast maturation

claim: Mitochondrial activity increases with cumulative hair cell activity.
source: These observations suggest that mitochondrial activity increases with cumulative hair cell activity.
evidence: Inference from mitoTimer data during neuromast maturation

claim: Younger hair cells lacking Hoechst labeling have a mitoTimer ratio near or below the median.
source: We found that younger hair cells lacking Hoechst labeling have a mitoTimer ratio near or below the median (Figure 4B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B

claim: Older hair cells that are positive for Hoechst labeling after 24 hr have mitoTimer ratios above the median.
source: The opposite is true for older hair cells that are positive for Hoechst labeling after 24 hr (Hoechst positive: 1.71 ± 0.52, n = 45 cells; Hoechst negative: 0.80 ± 0.45, n = 80 cells; Mann-Whitney U test, p < 0.001 ; mean ratio (normalized) ±SD; five fish per group).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B

claim: Cells with increased mitoTimer ratios are older and have been capable of MET activity for a longer period of time.
source: Together, these experiments suggest that cells with increased mitoTimer ratios are older and, as a result, have also been capable of MET activity for a longer period of time.
evidence: Inference from Hoechst labeling and mitoTimer data

claim: The mitoTimer fluorescence ratio was significantly decreased in sputnik mutants compared to age-matched WT/Het siblings, with a difference of 66.3%.
source: Compared to age-matched WT/Het siblings, the mitoTimer fluorescence ratio was significantly decreased in sputnik mutants, with a difference of 66.3% (Figure 5A–C; Mann-Whitney U test, p < 0.001; n = 14 WT/Het fish and 15 mutant fish; data combined from three experiments).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A-C

claim: Incubation in benzamil (200 μM) for 48 hr resulted in a reduction of mitoTimer fluorescence ratio of 43.4% relative to DMSO control.
source: Similar results were obtained when embryos were incubated in the MET-blocking drug benzamil (200 μM) for 48 hr (3-5dpf; Figure 5D–F) (Hailey et al., 2017). We observed a reduction of 43.4% relative to 0.5% DMSO control (Mann-Whitney U test, p < 0.001; n = 17 fish per group; data combined from two experiments).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5D-F

claim: Hair cell turnover is unchanged in the absence of MET activity.
source: The ratio of label retaining hair cells was consistent in both control and benzamil treated conditions, indicating that hair cell turnover is unchanged in the absence of MET activity (Figure 5—figure supplement 1; Control: 0.72 ± 0.12, n = 8 control fish; Treated: 0.70 ± 0.14, n = 10 fish).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1

claim: The percent decrease in red fluorescence of mitoEos was 38.9% for wildtype and 75.5% for mutants at 16 hr post-photoconversion.
source: While green fluorescence remained consistent (data not shown), the percent decrease in red fluorescence was 38.9% and 75.5% for wildtype and mutants, respectively (Mann-Whitney U test, p < 0.001; n = 9 fish per group).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6

claim: Mitochondrial or protein turnover increases with reduced hair cell activity.
source: The change in red fluorescence over time indicates that mitochondrial or protein turnover increases with reduced hair cell activity.
evidence: Inference from mitoEos photoconversion data

claim: Orbital rotation significantly increased the mitoTimer fluorescence ratio in WT/Het fish.
source: While orbital rotation significantly increased the mitoTimer fluorescence ratio in WT/Het fish, a statistically significant difference was not observed in age-matched sputnik mutants (WT/Het Control: 100 ± 34 n = 47 fish, WT/Het Orbital shaker: 128 ± 47 n = 48 fish, Mutant Control: 58 ± 24 n = 27 fish, Mutant Orbital shaker: 70 ± 21 n = 28 fish; Kruskal-Wallis test, Dunn's post-test, p < 0.05; mean ratio reported as a percent of WT/Het Control ± SD; data combined from four experiments) (Figure 7A, Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7A

claim: A statistically significant difference in mitoTimer fluorescence ratio was not observed in age-matched sputnik mutants after orbital rotation.
source: While orbital rotation significantly increased the mitoTimer fluorescence ratio in WT/Het fish, a statistically significant difference was not observed in age-matched sputnik mutants (WT/Het Control: 100 ± 34 n = 47 fish, WT/Het Orbital shaker: 128 ± 47 n = 48 fish, Mutant Control: 58 ± 24 n = 27 fish, Mutant Orbital shaker: 70 ± 21 n = 28 fish; Kruskal-Wallis test, Dunn's post-test, p < 0.05; mean ratio reported as a percent of WT/Het Control ± SD; data combined from four experiments) (Figure 7A, Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7A

claim: Orbital stimulation significantly increased the mitoTimer fluorescence of older, Hoechst-positive hair cells compared to control.
source: We observed that orbital stimulation significantly increased the red:green fluorescence of older, Hoechst-positive hair cells compared to control (Figure 7B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7B

claim: There was no significant difference in the mitoTimer fluorescence ratios of younger, Hoechst-negative cells in control and stimulated conditions.
source: Alternatively, there was no significant difference in the mitoTimer fluorescence ratios of younger, Hoechst-negative cells in both conditions (Hoechst-positive Control: 1.36 ± 0.37, n = 94 cells; Hoechst-negative Control: 0.90 ± 0.22, n = 52 cells; Hoechst-positive Orbital Shaker: 1.70 ± 0.47, n = 105 cells; Hoechst-negative Orbital Shaker: 0.97 ± 0.23, n = 77 cells; mean ratio ± SD; Kruskal-Wallis test, Dunn's post-test, p < 0.001; 10 fish per group).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7B

claim: The hair cells most affected by shaker stimulation are those that are already active before the onset of stimulation.
source: These results suggest that the hair cells most affected by shaker stimulation are those that are already active before the onset of stimulation.
evidence: Inference from Hoechst labeling and orbital shaker data

claim: Orbital shaking significantly increased CellROX fluorescence in WT/Het fish.
source: Similar to the mitoTimer fluorescent shift, orbital shaking significantly increased CellROX fluorescence in WT/Het fish (Figure 7C) (WT/Het Control: 100 ± 23 n = 20 fish, WT/Het Orbital shaker: 217 ± 124 n = 20 fish, Mutant Control: 105 ± 55 n = 21 fish, Mutant Orbital shaker: 138 ± 58 n = 20 fish; Kruskal-Wallis test, Dunn's post-test, p < 0.001; mean ratio reported as a percent of WT/Het Control ± SD; data combined from three experiments).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7C

claim: Cumulative mitochondrial activity and hair cell oxidation are influenced by long-term changes in MET activity.
source: These results demonstrate that cumulative mitochondrial activity and hair cell oxidation are influenced by long-term changes in MET activity.
evidence: Inference from mitoTimer and CellROX data with orbital shaking

claim: Analysis of JC-1 labelling did not reveal persistent changes in mitochondrial polarity after 24 hr of orbital shaking.
source: Unlike the cumulative mitochondrial and oxidative indicators, analysis of JC-1 labelling did not reveal persistent changes in mitochondrial polarity (Control: 0.52 ± 0.12, n = 10 fish; Orbital Shaker: 0.58 ± 0.11, n = 10 fish; mean ratio ±SD; Mann-Whitney U test, p = 0.32) (Figure 7D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7D

claim: Mitochondria are the source of ROS during neomycin-induced hair cell death following mitochondrial Ca2+ elevation.
source: Mitochondria play a key role, as a recent zebrafish study identified mitochondria as the source of ROS during neomycin-induced hair cell death following mitochondrial Ca2+ elevation (Esterberg et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Esterberg et al., 2016

claim: Mitigating mitochondrial ROS generation and Ca2+ uptake confers enhanced hair cell protection.
source: Moreover, mitigating mitochondrial ROS generation and Ca2+ uptake confers enhanced hair cell protection.
evidence: Supported by inference from cited literature

claim: Previous studies have noted selective and asynchronous hair cell death as a result of aminoglycoside exposure.
source: Previous studies have also noted selective and asynchronous hair cell death as a result aminoglycoside exposure, as well as variation in levels of ROS and Ca2+ in individual cells.
evidence: Supported by reference to previous studies

claim: There is no difference in the mean fluorescence ratios of living and dying cells measured by JC-1 just prior to neomycin exposure.
source: We observed no difference in the mean fluorescence ratios of living and dying cells using this measure (Living cells: 0.13 ± 0.14, n = 46; dying cells: 0.12 ± 0.11, n = 35; mean ratio ±SD; six fish, 2–3 neuromasts per fish; Mann-Whitney U test, p = 0.60) (Figure 8).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8

claim: Acute differences in mitochondrial activity just prior to neomycin exposure do not correspond with likelihood of subsequent hair cell death.
source: These results demonstrate that acute differences in mitochondrial activity just prior to neomycin exposure do not correspond with likelihood of subsequent hair cell death.
evidence: Inference from JC-1 experimental data

claim: The average mitoTimer ratio for surviving hair cells was below the median ratio at baseline, while the average ratio for cells that die following treatment was above the median.
source: We observed that the average mitoTimer ratio for surviving hair cells was below the median ratio at baseline, while the average ratio for cells that die following treatment was above the median (Figure 9B) (Live: 0.77 ± 0.37, Die: 1.30 ± 0.34; Mann-Whitney U test, p < 0.001; mean ratio (normalized) ±SD; n = 142 living cells, 74 dying cells from six fish; data combined from two experiments).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 9B

claim: A surviving cell had approximately an 85% chance of having a lower red:green ratio than a dying cell.
source: Comparing the two distributions, a surviving cell had approximately an 85% chance of having a lower red:green ratio than a dying cell.
evidence: Statistical analysis of mitoTimer data

claim: The red-green classification scheme provides a sensitivity of 0.78, specificity of 0.70, and a diagnostic odds ratio of 8.63.
source: This distribution shows that the red-green classification scheme provides a sensitivity of 0.78, specificity of 0.70, and a diagnostic odds ratio of 8.63, reflecting strong predictive value.
evidence: Statistical analysis of mitoTimer classification data

claim: Red cells are over eight-fold more likely to die than live after neomycin exposure.
source: In this case, the diagnostic odds ratio indicates that red cells are over eight-fold more likely to die than live after neomycin exposure.
evidence: Inference from diagnostic odds ratio calculation

claim: Older cells were more sensitive to 50 µM neomycin compared to younger cells.
source: Older cells were more sensitive to 50 µM neomycin compared to younger cells, as we reported previously (Santos et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by experimental data and citation to Santos et al., 2006

claim: For surviving hair cells, the mean red:green ratio was significantly lower than untreated controls for both older and younger cells.
source: For surviving hair cells – including both older hair cells, labeled with Hoechst, and younger unlabeled cells – the mean red:green ratio was significantly lower than untreated controls (Control Hoechst+: 1.03 ± 0.25 n = 124 cells; 50 μM Neo Hoechst+: 0.78 ± 0.23, n = 38 cells; 100 μM Neo Hoechst+: 0.76 ± 0.25, n = 8 cells; Control Hoechst-: 0.50 ± 0.09, n = 52 cells; 50 μM Neo Hoechst-: 0.45 ± 0.14, n = 64 cells; 100 μM Neo Hoechst-: 0.42 ± 0.12, n = 46 cells; mean ratio ± SD; nine fish per group).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 10B

claim: Cells with a higher mitoTimer ratio in both older and younger populations are more susceptible to damage.
source: These results suggest that cells with a higher mitoTimer ratio in both older and younger populations are more susceptible to damage.
evidence: Inference from neomycin treatment and mitoTimer data

claim: The most susceptible cells are the older and historically MET active cells in the cluster.
source: Together with our previous results, this suggests that the most susceptible cells are the older and historically MET active cells in the cluster.
evidence: Inference from combined experimental data on age and activity

claim: The cumulative history of mitochondrial activity in hair cells predicts their vulnerability to neomycin exposure.
source: In this way, the cumulative history of mitochondrial activity in hair cells predicts their vulnerability to neomycin exposure.
evidence: Inference from all mitoTimer and neomycin susceptibility data

claim: Mitochondrial Ca2+ buffering could be further investigated through manipulation of Ca2+ uptake and release mechanisms during hair cell stimulation.
source: Mitochondrial Ca2+ buffering could be further investigated through manipulation of Ca2+ uptake and release mechanisms during hair cell stimulation.
evidence: Speculation about future research directions

claim: ROS production within mitochondria occurs as a result of normal metabolic activity at two sites within the electron transport chain, complexes I and III.
source: ROS production within mitochondria occurs as a result of normal metabolic activity at two sites within the electron transport chain, complexes I and III.
evidence: Established knowledge about mitochondrial ROS production

claim: Electron leakage at complexes I and III leads to the generation of superoxide, which is converted into membrane-permeable hydrogen peroxide.
source: Electron leakage at these complexes leads to the generation of superoxide, which is converted into membrane-permeable hydrogen peroxide (Loschen et al., 1974; Turrens, 2003).
evidence: Supported by citations to studies on ROS generation

claim: Mitochondrial Ca2+ signaling can stimulate OXPHOS, and therefore, electron flow.
source: Mitochondrial Ca2+ signaling influences this process as it can stimulate OXPHOS, and therefore, electron flow (Brookes et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citation to Brookes et al., 2004

claim: Mitochondria may act as Ca2+ buffers, mediating Ca2+ homeostasis in addition to other means of cellular Ca2+ extrusion.
source: Compared to cytoplasmic Ca2+, the larger integrated area and rise time of the mitochondrial signal (Figure 1D,F) are consistent with the idea that mitochondria may act as Ca2+ buffers, mediating Ca2+ homeostasis in addition to other means of cellular Ca2+ extrusion.
evidence: Inference from experimental data on Ca2+ kinetics

claim: This role for hair cell mitochondria has been postulated in mammalian hair cells based on apical localization of the organelles and through Ca2+-imaging studies during transduction.
source: This role for hair cell mitochondria has been postulated in mammalian hair cells based, in part, on apical localization of the organelles and through Ca2+-imaging studies during transduction (Weaver and Schweitzer, 1994; Rüsch et al., 1998; Beurg et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to studies on mammalian hair cells

claim: mitoTimer red fluorescence shifts were observed in cultured myoblasts and Drosophila heart tube after treatment with agents known to increase mitochondrial ROS production.
source: mitoTimer red fluorescence shifts were observed in cultured myoblasts and Drosophila heart tube after treatment with agents known to increase mitochondrial ROS production, including rotenone, antimycin A, and paraquat.
evidence: Supported by reference to Laker et al., 2014 study

claim: A significant red shift in mitoTimer was observed in aging flies.
source: Additionally, the authors observed a significant red shift in aging flies, suggesting that mitoTimer reflects both the age and redox history of the organelles.
evidence: Supported by reference to Laker et al., 2014 study

claim: mitoTimer can be used to assess oxidative stress following ischemia-reperfusion injury in muscle.
source: Later studies also revealed that mitoTimer can be used to assess oxidative stress following ischemia-reperfusion injury in muscle (Wilson et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Wilson et al., 2019

claim: The formation of DsRed fluorescent protein is mediated by oxidation.
source: These findings are consistent with studies of the formation of DsRed fluorescent protein, which in itself is mediated by oxidation (Verkhusha et al., 2004; Yarbrough et al., 2001).
evidence: Supported by citations to studies on DsRed protein

claim: An important driving factor for mitochondrial import is mitochondrial membrane potential.
source: An important driving factor for mitochondrial import is mitochondrial membrane potential (Dudek et al., 2013; Wiedemann et al., 2004); however we did not observe a correspondence between potential and mitoTimer fluorescence ratio.
evidence: Supported by citations to studies on mitochondrial import

claim: A decrease in mitochondrial polarity in sputnik mutants was observed with JC-1 staining.
source: We observed a decrease in mitochondrial polarity in sputnik mutants with JC-1 staining, which in isolation would be predicted to result in an increase in the red:green ratio of mitoTimer, rather than the decrease we observed.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from JC-1 staining

claim: Increased mitochondrial turnover or turnover of protein occurs when MET activity is reduced.
source: Although this analysis provides only an estimate of turnover (based on the loss of photoconverted protein), our results suggest that increased mitochondrial turnover or turnover of protein occurs when MET activity is reduced (Figure 6), consistent with the observed changes in mitoTimer.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6

claim: Mitochondrial turnover via mitophagy occurs as a quality control process.
source: Previous studies have demonstrated mitochondrial turnover via mitophagy occurs as a quality control process (Campanella et al., 2009; Twig et al., 2008; Nowikovsky et al., 2007; Kim et al., 2007; Mizushima et al., 2003; Zhao et al., 2002).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to studies on mitophagy

claim: Increased OXPHOS activity has been associated with elongated mitochondrial morphology.
source: In other cell types, increased OXPHOS activity has been associated with elongated mitochondrial morphology and, in studies of isolated mitochondria, OXPHOS has been shown to stimulate fusion (reviewed Mishra and Chan (2016)Mishra and Chan, 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Mishra and Chan, 2016 review

claim: Mitochondrial activity and dynamics have been shown to reciprocally regulate each other.
source: The fact that mitochondrial activity and dynamics have been shown to reciprocally regulate each other suggests that mitoTimer could also reflect the interrelatedness of the two, as well as mitochondrial turnover via mitophagy.
evidence: Established knowledge about mitochondrial biology

claim: Reduced mitophagy has been observed with increased ROS in neurons.
source: Reduced mitophagy has been observed with increased ROS in neurons (Qi et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Qi et al., 2011

evidence: Supported by citations to studies on cochlear hair cell susceptibility
